lines.note: Hayashi here is musical accompaniment, not the grove sense at the end of f179. Deſcante and instrumental music define the new entry.
Hayashi wo suru means to perform this music. The wo marks hayashi as the object; the Portuguese translation continues on the next row.
Muſica completes the explanation of making the accompaniment. Its separate row is a physical continuation, not a new item.
Hayasu is the corresponding verb for musical performance. The printed abbreviated ending u is retained, although the full lexical form is hayasu.
Instruments and voices finish the musical definition. The separate right-hand '( uas &c.' completes er- in the following growth entry; it does not belong to the music.
This hayasu means to cause hair or plants to grow. Its er- is completed by the displaced uas above; the musical homograph must not control this interpretation.
This hayasu instead means to cut or carve. The register qualification begins Pala- here and is completed on the following row.
Palavra de molheres identifies the cutting sense as women's speech. This is the dictionary's historical usage classification, not a restriction imposed on the transcription.
Hayashimono is a dance accompanied by singing. The Portuguese subject continues into the group of people described on the next line.

runs.text: muitos que vão andando jũta mẽte. ¶

lines.note: Many people go along together while performing. The scan visibly abbreviates the latter expression as jũta mẽte; Fayaxi starts the Japanese example after the paragraph mark.
Mono wo suru completes hayashimono wo suru. The example concerns performing the dance or song described above, not an unrelated generic mono.
The performance is for festivity or spontaneous joy. Derepente is retained as joined in the source rather than regularized to modern de repente.
Hae here means destruction, explained by yaburi kobosu. It is a Sino-Japanese-looking destruction word, not the fish name in the next entry.
Hae ni oyobu means to come to destruction. The scan begins the Portuguese gloss with lowercase d; its sense confirms the cross-line Japanese phrase.
This separate hae names a fish, with no further identification. The generic gloss does not justify selecting a modern species.
Haye/hae is a verb of stretching or spreading here. The supplied uru gives hayuru; it should not be replaced by the modern haeru paradigm in Level 1.
Shikimono wo hayuru means to spread out a covering. Alcati- continues alcatifa 'carpet' below, giving a concrete example of the stretching/spreading sense.
The carpet or similar object completes the first example. Ito wo hayuru then introduces stretching thread, a second example of the same verb.

runs.text: Eſtender, ou eſtirar algum fio. ¶ Item, Na-

lines.note: The thread example is translated by extend or stretch. Item then opens the growth sense, whose Na- is continued below.
Na-çerem cabelos, eruas gives hair or plants growing. This is the intransitive counterpart of the growth sense of hayasu earlier on the page.
Haza means an interval of space or time. Itsu no haza ni introduces a question about the time available for an action.

runs.text: Quando, ou em q̃ tempo farei

lines.note: Kore wo shō ka means 'shall I do this?' The interrogative follows the time expression above; xô retains the source's closed long-vowel mark.

runs.text: iſto? No Cami ſe diz, Itçunomani.

lines.note: Isto closes the Portuguese question. Cami and itsu no ma ni are embedded Japanese terms here; both are set within italic prose in this scan.
Hazama is another interval word. The literary example begins uchi ni mo tsuwa-, continuing tsuwamono 'soldiers' on the next row.
The soldiers fill the place hima hazama mo nō: without gaps. The printed fima supports hima; monǒ contains mo plus contracted 'without,' not an independent modern mono.
Chite completes michimichite, 'filling completely,' before itta. Feiq. identifies the source, and lowercase lib. begins its book reference.

runs.text: dos dentro de maneira que eſtaua tudo cheo.

lines.note: The Portuguese says soldiers entered until everything was full. It corroborates the no-empty-space interpretation of the Japanese compound and contraction above.
Hazamaru means to be wedged or placed between things. The voiced z is the historical headword spelling and is not changed to modern hasamaru.
Entre duas couſas completes the intransitive definition. Only one additional displaced '( couſas.' is printed; it completes the following transitive entry, so the duplicate OCR copy is removed.
Hazame gives the transitive counterpart: insert or wedge between two things. Its final object couſas is the displaced fragment on the preceding row.
Hazu is an arrangement or agreement. Hazu wo awasuru illustrates fulfilling it; the Portuguese com- continues comprir below.
Comprir a promeſſa e concerto means fulfilling the promise or agreement. Fazuga begins a contrasting example with hazu as subject.
Hazu ga chigō means to differ from the arrangement or promise. The contracted chigō corresponds to chigau; no extra syllable should be supplied.
Another hazu wo awasuru sense concerns living up to expectations. The Portuguese fazer de peſ- must be read through the following row.

runs.text: ſoa, ou como ſe eſpera delle na guerra, &c.

lines.note: The explanation is to act as expected of a person, for example in war. This develops hazu as expected conduct rather than merely a negotiated promise.
Hazu no awanu hito describes someone who fails to meet an agreement or expectation. No is the subject-linking particle in the relative expression.

runs.text: cumpre com o que ficou, ou que não faz o que

lines.note: The person does not fulfill what was agreed or do what is required. This continues the relative clause explaining the Japanese description.

runs.text: deue conforme ao conceito que ſe tem de ſua

lines.note: The duty is measured against the opinion held of that person's abilities or character. Conceito here supplies that expectation, not a new abstract headword.
Peſſoa closes the account of someone failing expectations. The following hazu entry changes to the physical archery sense.
Hazu now denotes the bow's nock or notch. The example hazu wo tsu-gu is divided at the row end and concerns making or attaching it.

runs.text: Fazer a mauça doutra cana, corno, &c.

lines.note: Tsu-gu is completed before the explanation of making the notch from another cane or horn. Mauça is the source's technical Portuguese word and is preserved.
Hazu wo sasu concerns making the arrow nocks. Fre- continues frechas; the example must not be confused with putting a whole arrow on the string.

runs.text: chas com que as aſſentão na corda do arco.

lines.note: The notches let arrows sit on the bowstring. This clause explains their function and completes the preceding arrow-making example.
Hazumaki wo suru describes binding with thread. The compound's maki element and the Portuguese apertar com fio agree on wrapping or fastening.
The binding is next to the arrow's nock. This locative phrase finishes hazumaki rather than introducing a separate action.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de por a aljaua

lines.note: Hazudaka ni is an adverbial expression for placing the quiver high. The raised position is completed below and illustrated across the column break.

runs.text: com frechas na cinta alta, & eminente.

lines.note: The quiver with arrows is placed high at the belt. The Japanese example begins at the top of column 2 and should be read with this definition.
Nijǔxi is twenty-four, confirmed by the Portuguese numeral below; the scan has a marked u, not i. The decorated arrows are being placed hazudaka, with their nocks high.
Ni totte tsuqe completes the example crossing from column 1. Yax. is a roman citation label, while Tomando begins the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: aljaua em que tinha metidas 24. ſetas de pe-

lines.note: The quiver contains twenty-four arrows, corroborating nijǔshi above. The final pe- continues penas, the feathers described in the next row.

runs.text: nas com certas liſtras atraueſſadas, & pondoa

lines.note: The feathers have transverse stripes. Pondoa refers to putting the quiver in place, continuing the action expressed by totte tsuqe.

runs.text: na cinta de maneira q̃ ficaſe alta, & eminẽte.

lines.note: The quiver is placed at the belt so it stands high. This completes the explanation of hazudaka ni begun in the other column.

runs.text: Parte da ſeta junto da mauça que

lines.note: Hazumaki is the portion of the arrow beside its nock. The definition corresponds to the thread-wrapping example in column 1.
This part is tightened and wrapped with thread. The scan reads emburulhar, with an extra u compared with modern embrulhar; that historical form is retained.

runs.text: Certo caniuete com que abrem a mau-

lines.note: Hazusashi is a small knife used to open the bow's notch. The scan's technical context identifies a tool, not a verb phrase hazu sasu.

runs.text: ça do arco pera meter a corda. ¶ Itẽ, Qual-

lines.note: Mau-ça is completed before the purpose of inserting the bowstring. Item then broadens the word beyond this specialized use.

runs.text: quer caniuete, ou faca pequena de ponta aguda.

lines.note: Any small knife with a sharp point falls under the extended sense. Qual-quer crosses the preceding line break and is one Portuguese word.
Hazu names a purgative medicine in this entry. Fazer camaras refers to bowel evacuation in the dictionary's medical vocabulary, not constructing rooms.
Hazukashigaru is to feel or display embarrassment. Ter pejo and ver-gonha supply the paired Portuguese equivalents across this line break.
Gonha completes vergonha, 'shame' or 'embarrassment.' It belongs to the verb definition, not to the adjective printed next.

runs.text: Couſa de que ſe tem pejo, ou ver

lines.note: Hazukashii is something one feels shame about. A small mark above the first a may be an accent, also noted by NINJAL, but is too uncertain here to add to the diplomatic text.

runs.text: gonha. ¶ Item, Ter pejo, ou vergonha.

lines.note: The second adjective sense is simply to feel shame. This personal-predicate use explains why a Portuguese verbal gloss accompanies a Japanese adjective.
Hazukashisa is the abstract noun in -sa. The isolated derivative row inherits the embarrassment sense rather than needing a second gloss.
The contracted adverb appears with differently shaped u marks: Fazzucaxû, then Fazzucaxǔ vomô. The latter means to feel ashamed; its final vowel is not i.
Ter vergonha translates the preceding example. The displaced '( tro. S.' instead completes ou- on the following line, giving 'shame another person.'
Hazukashime is the verb for shaming someone else. Read ou- with the displaced tro above; the translation is not left with a missing object.
Hazumakasu means to hold the breath in this entry. It is distinguished from the intransitive hazumu immediately below by the causative-looking -akas- form.
Iki wo hazumakasu repeats the breath-holding sense. The object marker wo and Portuguese deter agree, with dei- beginning the alternative explanation.
Dei-xar de respirar completes 'cease breathing.' This is a linguistic gloss of the example, not an instruction or modern medical description.
Hazumu here concerns breath being stopped or impeded. The historical sense should not be replaced with only the modern ball-bouncing meaning.
The person cannot catch breath and is stifled. Iki ga begins the intransitive Japanese example, with its verb on the following short row.
The scan reads fazzumu, completing iki ga hazumu. The OCR fazzuiu failed to recognize the m; the headword paradigm and breath gloss support the correction.
This separate hazumu entry describes a ball bouncing. Ma- begins mari, the ball that is subject of the example below.
Mari ga hazumu completes the bouncing-ball example. Item then introduces a horse moving excitedly, starting aluo- before the next row.
Aluo-raçado and brincando explain the horse's lively movement. Uma no opens a longer literary example whose reins and movement are described below.
Uma no ashi no oyobō hodo wa concerns how far the horse's feet reach. Tazuna wo kurete means giving or letting out the reins; the Portuguese below supports it.
Ayumasei is an imperative causative 'make it walk'; hazumaba is conditional. Tazuna wo cutte contrasts drawing in the reins with letting them out.
Oyogasei is 'make it swim,' not an unrelated malformed walking verb. The Feiq. citation and Portuguese nadar below support that reading in this horse passage.

runs.text: dar o caualo largando lhe as redeas quanto elle

lines.note: The translation says to let the horse move while giving it rein as far as it can. The explicit horse object links this to the longer Japanese example.

runs.text: poder, & ſe for muito apreſſado puxando lhe

lines.note: If it becomes too hurried, the rider draws on the reins. This corresponds to the Japanese conditional hazumaba and tazuna wo cutte.
The Portuguese explicitly ends 'make it swim.' The unusual action is therefore retained rather than normalizing oyogasei to a more expected walking command.

runs.text: Loro do cabreſto com que amarrão o

lines.note: Hazuna is a halter strap for tying a horse. Initial f belongs to the historical ha-series transcription, not modern tazuna imposed from the earlier example.
The horse is tied in the stable. Cavallo is printed with doubled l here, unlike some nearby instances of caualo, and is retained.

runs.text: Duas amarras com que tem mão no

lines.note: A separate hazuna entry concerns two mooring ropes holding a vessel. The nautical definition prevents treating it as another horse strap example.

runs.text: nauio, hũa dellas eſta no mar com a fateixa, &

lines.note: One rope is in the sea with the grapnel or anchor. The paired structure hũa ... outra continues on the following row.
The other rope is at the stern. This short continuation completes the two-part nautical description.

runs.text: Borde, ou arrabalde fora dalgũa po-

lines.note: Hazure means an edge or outskirts beyond a settlement. Borde is retained as the visible Portuguese form rather than modernized to borda.
The example is mura or machi hazure ni, 'on the outskirts of a village or town.' Final ni is visible, not the OCR m; the next row's sumu confirms the locative construction.

runs.text: Morar fora, ou nos arrabaldes da vila,

lines.note: Sumu completes 'live on the outskirts.' Morar fora and arrabaldes provide a direct bilingual check on hazure ni above.
Ou pouoação completes the reference to a village or settlement. This closes the noun entry before the related verb begins.
Hazururu means to deviate or be out of alignment. Mi- starts michi in the first example, not a separate short headword.
Michi ni hazururu is to stray from the road. The next example starts Fat-, completing hatto 'law' below.
Hatto ni hazururu means not to keep the law. Fito- begins the final example, which develops departure from ordinary human behavior.
Hitonami ni hazururu means to depart from the ordinary run of people. The Portuguese says to be singular or not go along with others; its last phrase continues below and onto f181.
This right-aligned com continues 'não ir com' in the preceding gloss. It is retained as the supplied body continuation, with the rest of the sentence on the next page.
